Locus Circle

GeometryCirclesAlgebra
What it shows: This is a picture, not a game: it shows every place for P that is always the same number of times as far from A as from B.
How to play: Drag A, B or P, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Change the two number boxes, tick the boxes to see the guide lines, and press Reset.
Look for the math

Drag P around and the distance to A divided by the distance to B never changes. The whole path is one circle — except when the two numbers are equal, when it becomes a straight line.

Two numbered points on AB

Set the two boxes to NB and NC, and write r = NB/NC. The applet marks M between A and B with AM/BM = r, and N outside AB with AN/BN = r. Those are the feet of the internal and external angle bisectors of triangle APB. Here M divides AB into NB and NC parts and N is built the same way from the difference; the logic test checks AM/BM = AN/BN = r for all 225 pairs of numbers.

Why MN is a diameter

The bisectors at P meet AB at M and N, so PM and PN are at right angles. By Thales' theorem a right angle subtends a diameter, so the circle on MN as diameter is exactly the circle of Apollonius. Its centre is A + r²/(r²−1)·(B−A) and its radius is r·AB/|r²−1|. The test confirmed both formulas and sampled thousands of points on the circle: every one has AP/BP = r.

Many circles, one family

All the circles for different values of r form the Apollonian family. No two of them cross, and they crowd around A when r is small and around B when r is large. The applet's own page says smaller r moves near B; the formula and 210 circles show the opposite, and the test checks it. Tick Extra construction to see the locus circle drawn in full.

What happens when the numbers match

When NB = NC we have r = 1. There is no finite circle: the locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB. The old applet put N a million pixels away, which only looks right when AB is level; with a slanted AB it is off by nearly 18 pixels. This page draws the exact line, as the article says. Tick Hint to see the pink parallels that carry the division from AB to P and to N.

Set both boxes to the same number, then drag B: P stays on the line that cuts AB in half at a right angle.
